newsitem.title: GEORGIA: IMF wants tax, bank reforms in ex-Soviet Georgia.
newsitem.headline: IMF wants tax, bank reforms in ex-Soviet Georgia.

text.p: The former Soviet republic of Georgia needs to improve banking and tax reforms to receive the next tranche of an $80 million International Monetary Fund credit for 1997, an IMF official said on Thursday.

Mohammad-Shadman Valavi, leader of an IMF delegation in Georgia that is reviewing Tbilisi's progress in implementing reforms, told Reuters the IMF board would discuss on March 19 disbursement of the $40 million tranche.
Georgia's parliament is considering changes to tax laws -- including exemptions for enterprises and certain sectors from a 20 percent value-added tax -- which has upset the IMF.
"The IMF will have a problem with Georgia if parliament adds more exemptions to the VAT law," Valavi said.
He said there were doubts over whether the state could collect tax revenues as envisioned in the 1997 budget.
But he said the Georgian economy had improved and assessed positively the stability of the national currency, the lari, and control over inflation, which is less than one percent a month.
"In many areas, Georgia is energetically moving forward with reforms," he said.
Total ESAF lending to the Caucasus country over 1996-1998 is scheduled at $240 million.
